title: Future forms in context: cumulative review
objectives: Choose a future form for a stated context.
Distinguish a schedule from an arrangement.
Review present perfect and past simple forms.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: English has several ways to talk about the future. The choice depends on how the speaker presents the situation. We often use will for an immediate decision or an opinion about the future: ‘The phone is ringing. I'll answer it’ and ‘I think our team will win’. We often use be going to for an intention formed before speaking: ‘I'm going to learn to drive’.

The present continuous can describe an arrangement, often one involving another person or booking: ‘I'm meeting my tutor on Tuesday’. The present simple can present a future event as part of a timetable: ‘The train leaves at six’. These descriptions are useful starting points; more than one form can be possible in some real contexts.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Will is followed by the base form: ‘She will travel’. For a negative, use will not or won't: ‘She won't travel’. For a question, put will before the subject: ‘Will she travel?’ Use am, is or are plus going to and a base verb for an intention: ‘We are going to travel’. The verb be changes according to the subject.

For a present continuous arrangement, use am, is or are plus an -ing form: ‘They are travelling tomorrow’. In the present simple timetable pattern, use the ordinary present form: ‘The bus leaves at eight’. For a timetable question, use does with a singular subject: ‘What time does the bus leave?’

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: A single trip can be described in different ways. ‘I've booked a table; I'm having dinner with my sister on Friday’ presents the dinner as arranged. ‘The restaurant opens at six’ gives a published opening time. ‘I'm going to order the fish’ can express an intention already formed; ‘I'll have the soup’ can be a decision made while ordering.

This review also revisits the present perfect and past simple. ‘I've visited Rome’ reports experience without a finished date; ‘I visited Rome in 2022’ places the visit in a finished past period. ‘I've lived here for three years’ can describe a situation that began in the past and continues now.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: A plan does not guarantee an outcome. ‘I'm going to apply’ reports an intention, not a promise that the application will be successful. Similarly, a timetable can change. The present simple presents a time as scheduled; it does not mean a delay is impossible.

Do not mix the structures: say ‘She is going to study’, not ‘She going to study’; and ‘The train leaves’, not ‘The train leave’. In practice, speakers may choose different forms to emphasise different aspects of the same event. Exercise instructions specify a form or situation when more than one answer would otherwise be defensible.

examples.note: The present continuous presents an arrangement.

examples.note: The present simple presents a timetable.
The present perfect reports experience without a finished date.
The past simple gives a finished past time.

common_errors.reason: A form of be is needed before going to.

common_errors.incorrect: I have visited Rome last year.
common_errors.reason: Use the past simple with the finished time last year.

summary: Use future forms according to the meaning and context.
Will, going to, present continuous and present simple can all refer to the future.
Review present perfect experience and past simple finished time.

exercises.prompt: The phone is ringing. I decide now: I ___ it.
exercises.explanation: Will answer expresses the immediate decision.

option_feedback.a: “answer yesterday” does not fit here. Will answer expresses the immediate decision.
option_feedback.b: “am answer” does not fit here. Will answer expresses the immediate decision.
option_feedback.c: “will answers” does not fit here. Will answer expresses the immediate decision.
option_feedback.d: “will answer” fits here. Will answer expresses the immediate decision.

option_feedback.b: “leaving” does not fit here. Leaves presents the timetable with a singular subject.
option_feedback.c: “leave” does not fit here. Leaves presents the timetable with a singular subject.
option_feedback.d: “left” does not fit here. Leaves presents the timetable with a singular subject.

exercises.prompt: We booked a table. We ___ dinner there tomorrow. Use the present continuous.

option_feedback.a: “have yesterday” does not fit here. Are having presents the booked arrangement.

option_feedback.c: “is have” does not fit here. Are having presents the booked arrangement.
option_feedback.d: “having” does not fit here. Are having presents the booked arrangement.

exercises.prompt: I formed an intention earlier: I ___ learn French next year.
exercises.explanation: Am going to expresses the prior intention.

option_feedback.a: “am” does not fit here. Am going to expresses the prior intention.
option_feedback.b: “will to” does not fit here. Am going to expresses the prior intention.
option_feedback.c: “am going to” fits here. Am going to expresses the prior intention.
option_feedback.d: “am going” does not fit here. Am going to expresses the prior intention.

exercises.prompt: They ___ to York in 2020.
exercises.explanation: Went places the visit in a finished year.

option_feedback.a: “have been” does not fit here. Went places the visit in a finished year.
option_feedback.b: “have went” does not fit here. Went places the visit in a finished year.
option_feedback.c: “go” does not fit here. Went places the visit in a finished year.
option_feedback.d: “went” fits here. Went places the visit in a finished year.

exercises.prompt: She has lived here ___ 2021 and still lives here.
exercises.explanation: Since introduces a starting year.

option_feedback.a: “for” does not fit here. Since introduces a starting year.
option_feedback.b: “ago” does not fit here. Since introduces a starting year.
option_feedback.c: “since” fits here. Since introduces a starting year.
option_feedback.d: “last” does not fit here. Since introduces a starting year.
